findings.title: Any web origin can materialize a privileged 127.0.0.1:5137 document via the SPA fallback and drive the REAL domain-approval prompt with a self-chosen domain — one click grants persistent auto-approve
findings.mechanism: The G1 fix hardened WHICH URL reaches the handler but not WHO may request it. `SimpleHandler::GetResourceRequestHandler` gates solely on `hodos::IsInternalFrontendUrl(request URL) && IsFrontendAvailable(...)`; it never consults `role_`, the initiating frame, or `request_initiator`. So a tab rendering https://evil.com can navigate itself (`location = 'http://127.0.0.1:5137/brc100-auth?type=domain_approval&domain=evil.com'`) — no gesture, no mixed-content block (loopback is potentially-trustworthy), no PNA (top-level navigation), and no listening server needed. `LocalFileResourceRequestHandler::GetResourceHandler` finds no file named `brc100-auth`, takes the SPA fallback, and returns `{app}\frontend\index.html` (macOS: `Contents/Resources/frontend/index.html`) as `text/html` via the 2-arg `CefStreamResourceHandler(mime, stream)` — the 'default response values' ctor, so status 200 with an EMPTY header map: no CSP, no `X-Frame-Options`, no `frame-ancestors`. The document therefore commits at origin `127.0.0.1:5137`, which every trust predicate accepts as wallet-internal: `IsInternalOrigin("127.0.0.1:5137")` returns true, so the C2 default-deny IPC gate is bypassed wholesale (not just the 4-name allowlist), and `cefMessage` is injected on EVERY V8 context (`global->SetValue("cefMessage", ...)` sits outside the `isInternalPage || isOverlayBrowser` block). `main.tsx` uses `BrowserRouter`, so React routes on the attacker-supplied path; `BRC100AuthOverlayRoot`'s `applyParams` reads `window.location.search` for `type` and `domain`, and the `notificationType === 'domain_approval'` branch renders the genuine '<domain> wants to connect to your wallet' card. `handleAllow` then sends `add_domain_permission` with `{domain: notificationDomain, identityKeyDisclosureAllowed, bundledScopeGrant}` — and the C++ arm at `simple_handler.cpp` line 4967 takes `permData["domain"]` verbatim, with NO pending-request binding, no role check, and no comparison against any frame. `identityKeyDisclosureAllowed` and `bundledScopeGrant` both default true. The sibling `add_domain_permission_advanced` arm (reachable from the same card's DomainPermissionForm) additionally accepts caller-supplied `perTxLimitCents` / `perSessionLimitCents` / `rateLimitPerMin` / `maxTxPerSession`. Net: a site can raise its OWN approval dialog, on its own schedule, with all trust chrome correct because the dialog is authentic, and one click yields persistent auto-approve + identity-key disclosure + bundled scope grant. Without the SPA fallback the `/brc100-auth` request would fall through to the network and hit connection-refused in production — the fallback is the load-bearing step.

lenses.ruledOut:
All CODE_READING; I am on Windows and built/ran nothing, so nothing below is MEASURED.

**macOS/Windows parity of the G1 predicate — CLEAN.** There is exactly ONE construction site of `LocalFileResourceRequestHandler` in the whole tree (`simple_handler.cpp :: SimpleHandler::GetResourceRequestHandler`) and exactly one `IsFrontendAvailable` call, and `src/handlers/simple_handler.cpp` sits in the shared (non-`if(APPLE)`) SOURCES list in `cef-native/CMakeLists.txt`. Both the `#ifdef _WIN32` and `#ifdef __APPLE__` include arms pull in `LocalFileResourceHandler.h`. There is no `GetResourceRequestHandler` override in `simple_handler_mac.mm`. So macOS reaches the identical `hodos::IsInternalFrontendUrl` — the Windows-only-fix concern the lens raised does not hold. (The macOS arm IS live on shipping builds: `release.yml` copies `frontend/dist/*` into `Contents/Resources/frontend/`, so `IsFrontendAvailable` returns true there.)

**Path traversal out of `frontend/` — could not break it.** `ExtractPath` never percent-decodes, and `url_` is `request->GetURL().ToString()`, i.e. a GURL-canonical spec. Chromium's path canonicalizer treats `%2e`/`%2E` as a dot for dot-segment resolution and unescapes unnecessary escapes of path-safe characters, so `/../`, `/%2e%2e/`, and `/.%2e/` are all resolved away before the handler sees them; anything that survives as a literal (`a%2F..%2F..%2Fx`) still contains the substring `..` and is caught by `url_path.find(\"..\")`. Double-encoding (`%252e%252e`) survives canonicalization but is never decoded by the handler, so it names a literal directory and fails to open. Rooted paths (`/x`, `//host/share`, `///x`) are caught by the `url_path[0]=='\\\\' || '/'` check — note the Windows `std::replace('/'→'\\\\')` runs before that check, so both spellings are covered. Drive-absolute (`C:/…`) is caught by `url_path[1]==':'`; `C|` is not a Win32 drive separator. UNC/`\\\\?\\` need a leading separator and are blocked. Residual risk is structural, not exploitable today: the guard is a raw substring/prefix test that is only safe because the input is guaranteed canonical — if a future call site ever hands this class a non-canonical string, re-audit.

**Symlinks / HFS+ / APFS case-insensitivity — no vector found.** `base_dir_` is inside our own app bundle (`Contents/MacOS/../Resources/frontend/`), which is not attacker-writable, so there is no symlink to plant. Case-insensitive lookup only lets an attacker reach files that are already reachable under their real names. Trailing dots/spaces and NTFS ADS (`index.html:$DATA`) give no escape either.

**Host-form spoofing of the predicate — fails closed, correctly.** `http://localhost.:5137/`, `http://[::1]:5137/`, `http://127.0.0.1:51370/`, `http://127.0.0.1:5137@evil/` all miss `IsInternalFrontendUrl`, and `IsInternalOrigin`'s `matchesHostOrHostColon` agrees, so the two predicates do not disagree in the dangerous direction. GURL normalizes the numeric-IP aliases (`2130706433`, `0177.0.0.1`, port `05137`) to the real loopback form, which is genuinely internal — not a bypass.

**Frontend postMessage handlers.** `grep` for `event.origin` / `e.origin` finds zero occurrences in `frontend/src/**` (only prose in CLAUDE.md files), so none of the ~12 `window.addEventListener('message', …)` handlers validates the sender. I chased each one anyway and they are all display-state updates (`wallet_shown`/`wallet_resize` panel height, `find_result`, `tab_list_response`, `payment_indicator`, download state, QR result pre-filling a form that still requires the user to press Send). I could not find a handler that performs a privileged action on message receipt, so I am NOT reporting the missing origin checks as an exploit — only as a latent hazard that becomes one the moment a handler gains a side effect, given finding #1 makes an attacker-held handle to an internal-origin frame possible.

**Other URL-param-driven internal routes.** `WalletOverlayRoot` (`?tab=`, range-clamped), `PrivacyShieldOverlayRoot` (`?domain=`, display only), `WalletPanel` (`?ppc`/`?ppa`, a banner), `ProfilePickerOverlayRoot` (`?mode=window`), `CertErrorPage`, `PaymentPendingPage`/`PaymentFailedPage` — none sends a privileged IPC on mount from URL data; `/brc100-auth` is the only one whose params reach an IPC, and only via a user click.

**MIME handling.** `GetMimeForPath` is applied to the requested path, but the SPA fallback correctly hard-codes `text/html`, so there is no content-type-confusion trick (e.g. requesting `/x.js` and being served index.html as JavaScript).

Not in this lens and deliberately not re-derived: the deferred disclosure set, the 73 ungateable Rust routes, `is_permission_surface` being a string list, and the macOS `wallet_call` SSRF.

lenses.lens: macOS overlay creation and lifecycle (cef_browser_shell_mac.mm, OverlayHelpers_mac.mm) vs the Windows equivalents in simple_app.cpp — hunting for remote-URL overlays, missing role assignments, dApp-shim injection into an overlay, keep-alive/destroy asymmetries, and Windows-only security checks absent on macOS.

findings.title: macOS BRC-100 auth overlay is created with role "brc100_auth" while every consumer keys on "brc100auth" — the browser is never registered and the auth-data/API-injection arms are silently skipped (fails closed; likely dead path)
findings.mechanism: cef_browser_shell_mac.mm :: CreateBRC100AuthOverlayWithSeparateProcess constructs `new SimpleHandler("brc100_auth")` (line 3501, underscore). Every consumer keys on the no-underscore spelling "brc100auth": BrowserWindow::SetBrowserForRole/GetBrowserForRole (BrowserWindow.cpp) have only a `role == "brc100auth"` branch; SimpleHandler::OnAfterCreated calls `owner_win->SetBrowserForRole(role_, browser)` with role_="brc100_auth" → no matching branch → NO-OP, so BrowserWindow::brc100_auth_browser stays null and GetBRC100AuthBrowser() (reads that member) returns null on macOS. Consequently OnLoadingStateChange's `else if (role_ == "brc100auth")` arm (simple_handler.cpp ~1325) — which calls InjectHodosBrowserAPI(browser) and schedules sendAuthRequestDataToOverlay() — never runs for this overlay, and sendAuthRequestDataToOverlay() would in any case find a null browser and log "Auth browser not available." The overlay_close role-clearing and force-shutdown CloseBrowser (mac line 4879-4891) also see null. Windows spells it "brc100auth" consistently (simple_app.cpp:1108), so the divergence is macOS-only. Direction of failure is CLOSED: with no hodosBrowser API and no auth data, the overlay cannot render or emit an approve/reject IPC, so no funds move and no secret is disclosed to web content. The path is additionally near-dead: it is reached only via the overlay_show_brc100_auth IPC, sent from initWindowBridge.ts only when window.pendingBRC100AuthRequest is set, and nothing in the tree ever sets that property (grep: only a read and a null-assignment). The live money-path approval modal is the separate "notification" overlay, whose role string IS consistent on both platforms.
findings.experiment: On a macOS build, trigger the legacy overlay by evaluating in a page: `window.cefMessage.send('overlay_show_brc100_auth',['evil.com','POST','/createAction','{}','domain_approval'])`. Expected observable on macOS: log shows the overlay window created but then "🔐 Auth browser not available for sending data" from sendAuthRequestDataToOverlay, and the overlay never receives the `brc100_auth_request` process message (React shows no request). On the same experiment on Windows you instead get "🔐 Sent auth request data to overlay". Confirms GetBRC100AuthBrowser() is null on macOS due to the role-string mismatch. Fix: change the mac literal to "brc100auth" (or add "brc100_auth" branches everywhere). Because the trigger property is never set in production and the failure is closed, this is a latent correctness/lifecycle divergence, not an exploit.

lenses.ruledOut: Read cef_browser_shell_mac.mm and OverlayHelpers_mac.mm end to end and diffed every Create*OverlayMacOS/Create*OverlayWithSeparateProcess against simple_app.cpp. No exploit found. (1) NO REMOTE-URL OVERLAY: every macOS overlay CreateBrowser loads http://127.0.0.1:5137/<page> (settings, privacy-shield/cookie, wallet-panel, backup, brc100-auth, menu, omnibox, downloads, profile-picker, bookmarks, site-info, tab-list, notification); the only non-5137 URLs are the /shutdown POST and saved-tab restore, neither an overlay. No overlay can navigate to a remote origin from its creator. (2) dApp SHIM NOT INJECTED INTO OVERLAYS: the window.CWI/yours/panda + wallet_call transport shim is gated in the SHARED render process (simple_render_process_handler.cpp :: OnContextCreated) by URL — `isExternalPage = !hodos::IsLoopbackUrl(url) && !hodos::IsInternalFrontendUrl(url)` plus https-only and main-frame-only. Overlays load loopback:5137, so they are excluded identically on both platforms; this file is not platform-forked. (3) IPC TRUST GATE IS SHARED: the default-deny gate (SimpleHandler::OnProcessMessageReceived → ResolveIpcOrigin + IpcMessageAllowedFromWebPage) lives in simple_handler.cpp and runs on macOS unchanged; hodos::OriginFromUrl userinfo/scheme hardening (PortConfig.h) is header-shared. (4) NOTIFICATION OVERLAY (the real money-path modal) uses role \"notification\" consistently on macOS — InjectHodosBrowserAPI + approve/reject IPC + keep-alive hide all intact (simple_handler.cpp OnLoadingStateChange/overlay_close mac arms). (5) BROWSER SETTINGS: mac overlays enable only javascript / clipboard / dom_paste — no web_security-off, no universal/file access, no remote-fonts loosening. Two NON-security divergences noted but not findings: (a) the mac wallet overlay creator does NOT set g_wallet_overlay_prevent_close=true synchronously at creation the way Windows CreateWalletOverlay does — a mnemonic/PIN screen could be dismissed slightly more eagerly on click-outside, but the mnemonic is shown to the USER, never disclosed to web content, so it is a UX-robustness gap, not a secret-to-web leak; (b) the mac wallet creator destroy-and-recreates and closes the old NSWindow without calling CloseBrowser on the prior windowless CEF browser (a resource leak), but the orphaned browser is not addressable by web content.

findings.title: /wallet/certificate/publish and /wallet/certificate/unpublish are page-reachable fund-movers with NO gate of any kind — publish_certificate calls create_action_internal DIRECTLY, skipping create_action's dispatch_payment and its per-tx defense-in-depth
findings.mechanism: An approved dApp origin runs `cefMessage.send('wallet_call',[id,'x','/wallet/certificate/unpublish',body,'POST'])`. The wallet_call arm of SimpleHandler::OnProcessMessageReceived applies NO endpoint allowlist — it forwards the page-supplied `endpoint` string verbatim to HandleIpcWalletCall, and runIpcEngineCascade builds `hodos::WalletBaseUrl() + endpoint` and stamps X-Requesting-Domain. domain_trust_mw waves an APPROVED domain through, and is_permission_surface does not cover /wallet/certificate/. Both handlers are declared `(state, req: web::Json<PublishCertificateRequest>, _body: web::Bytes)` — NO HttpRequest, so they structurally cannot gate themselves (the known-open 73-route bucket). The NEW facet: these two are not disclosure routes, they BROADCAST. unpublish_certificate_core hand-builds a tx with a `TxOutput::new(HODOS_SERVICE_FEE_SATS, fee_script)` output plus miner fee and broadcasts it; publish_certificate builds a CreateActionRequest with `no_send: Some(false)` and calls `create_action_internal` DIRECTLY — bypassing create_action entirely, which is a stronger form of the very TestRequest anti-pattern this lens was sent to audit (it does not even pass a synthetic request; it skips the gated wrapper). Result: an approved dApp can loop publish→unpublish and burn ~2x(1000 sats + miner fee) per cycle from the user's wallet to the Hodos treasury with no modal, no per-tx cap, no per-session cap, no rate limit and no gold pill. Precondition: the user holds at least one identity certificate.

findings.title: /acquireCertificate and /sendMessage are listed in IsPaymentEndpoint but have no body shape in ExtractOutputSatoshis — the exact 'do both or neither' violation the file's own banner declares fatal, and payment_cost_test.cpp codifies only the harmless half
findings.mechanism: PaymentCost.h's banner states: 'Listing an endpoint in the first without teaching the second its body shape prices the call at 0 cents, which the engine reads as under every cap and SILENTLY AUTO-APPROVES (matrix_c.rs :: bsv_price_available_with_zero_cents_is_silent asserts exactly that). Do both or neither — this is the d33741a rule.' IsPaymentEndpoint returns true for /createAction, /acquireCertificate, /sendMessage, /transaction/send, /wallet/peerpay/send, /wallet/paymail/send, /processAction — seven endpoints. ExtractOutputSatoshis knows FOUR body shapes (outputs[].satoshis, amount, amount_satoshis, sendMax) and its own comment says so ('FOUR body shapes, because four endpoint families reach here'). /acquireCertificate's body ({acquisitionProtocol, type, certifier, fields, certifierUrl}) and /sendMessage's body ({recipient, messageBox, body}) match none of them, so `shapes == 0` and the function returns 0. ComputePaymentCost then sets priceAvailable = (bsvPriceUsd > 0) = true with cents = 0. dispatch_payment builds PaymentCall{cents:0, bsv_price_available:true} from the headers and matrix_c returns Silent(SilentWithinCaps) — verified by the cited unit test at matrix_c.rs line 782. So both endpoints receive an unconditional Silent decision that has considered no amount at all. Compounding it: tests/payment_cost_test.cpp asserts `EXPECT_TRUE(hodos::IsPaymentEndpoint("/acquireCertificate"))` and the same for /sendMessage, but contains NO ExtractOutputSatoshis row for either body — the suite locks in the half of the rule that carries no money and omits the half that does, so it would stay green with the pricing half of the rule entirely absent.

findings.title: X-User-Approved approvals are not bound to the endpoint they were minted for, and today's change made one body hash simultaneously valid at a create-only and a create+sign+BROADCAST endpoint
findings.mechanism: PendingApproval stores `endpoint` and consume_and_verify's caller logs `approval.endpoint`, but consume_and_verify's signature is `(approval_id, body, now)` and its body performs exactly three checks — map removal, expires_at, and sha256(body) == body_hash. The endpoint is never compared to the endpoint currently being gated. Before today that was mostly academic because the gated payment endpoints took disjoint body shapes. It is no longer: ProcessActionRequest deserializes {outputs, description, labels, broadcast} and, having no deny_unknown_fields, silently ignores `options`, `inputs`, `inputBEEF`, `lockTime` and `version` — so a body that is a valid CreateActionRequest is byte-for-byte a valid ProcessActionRequest. One (domain, body_hash) approval minted at /createAction therefore satisfies the replay check at /processAction and vice versa. I could NOT find a delivery vector: tryHandlePendingResponse stores modalCtx.endpoint from the ORIGINAL request and resumeInternalResponse re-issues to that endpoint with resume.headersOnApprove["X-User-Approved"], the page never sees approvalId (the 202 envelope is intercepted in C++), and the fetch path strips x-user-approved from page-supplied headers via kTrustHeaderExact. Double replay is prevented — consume_and_verify does `guard.remove(approval_id)` before any check, so NotFound on the second attempt. So this is a missing binding, NOT a live exploit; it is one C++ refactor (or one path that echoes a 202 body to the page) away from becoming one.

findings.title: /processAction is single-layered where /createAction is double-layered: the inner TestRequest makes check_domain_approved return Ok(None), so create_action's Rust-side per-tx cap re-check never runs for a processAction spend
findings.mechanism: create_action carries a second, independent cap check after dispatch_payment: it calls `check_domain_approved(&http_req, ...)`, and on Ok(Some(perm)) recomputes `total_sats` from req.outputs, prices it against the live BSV price, and 403s ERR_SPENDING_LIMIT_EXCEEDED if it exceeds perm.per_tx_limit_cents — plus 403 ERR_PRICE_UNAVAILABLE when no price is available. This is the Rust-side backstop against a C++ ExtractOutputSatoshis mis-price. process_action calls create_action with `actix_web::test::TestRequest::default().to_http_request()`, which carries no X-Requesting-Domain, so check_domain_approved hits its `Ok(None) => {}` arm (handlers.rs:4425) and the ENTIRE defense-in-depth block is skipped. Net effect of today's fix: /processAction now has exactly one gate where /createAction has two, over an endpoint that additionally BROADCASTS. Any future divergence between nlohmann's read of the body and serde's — the decoy-key/nested-sendMax family, a new CreateActionOutput alias, a shape added to ProcessActionRequest — is caught at /createAction and not at /processAction, making /processAction the strictly cheaper endpoint at which to exploit any such drift. This is a structural observation about the fix, not a claim that a divergence exists today; I looked for one and did not find one (see ruledOut).

lenses.ruledOut:
Everything below I checked and found SOUND. All of it is CODE_READING on a Windows box; I ran no wallet and no browser, so nothing here is MEASURED.

1. DECOY-KEY FAMILY against /processAction — CLEAN. I enumerated every field ExtractOutputSatoshis reads (outputs[].satoshis, amount, amount_satoshis, sendMax, options.sendMax) against every field ProcessActionRequest reads (outputs, description, labels, broadcast). Every decoy pushes C++ toward FAIL-CLOSED, never toward under-pricing: `{"outputs":[{"satoshis":1e8}],"amount":1}` sets shapes==2 → kAmountNotDerivable → price_unavailable PROMPT; `{"outputs":[],"amount":1}` prices the decoy at 1 sat but ProcessActionRequest.outputs is then empty so nothing is spent beyond the service fee. The panel-#2 empty-array carve-out ("an EMPTY outputs array is not a shape at all") is what makes the first decoy variant impossible here. I found no body that prices low and spends high.

2. NEGATIVE / OVERFLOWING SATOSHIS — REFUTED as a money-mover. CreateActionOutput.satoshis is Option<i64> (signed, no positivity check anywhere in create_action_internal), so `[{satoshis:1e8},{satoshis:-99999999}]` does price at 1 sat. But C++ (`total += get<int64_t>()`) and Rust (`total_output += sats`; and create_action's backstop `filter_map(|o| o.satoshis).sum()`) sum with sign IDENTICALLY, so there is no divergence to exploit, and the resulting transaction carries a negative-value output that no broadcaster accepts — the failure path restores inputs via `restore_spent_by_txid` and disables the ghost change output. No money moves. i64 overflow wraps the same way on both sides (nlohmann static_cast, Rust release wrapping).

3. TYPE-CONFUSION BETWEEN THE TWO PARSERS — CLEAN, because both must succeed. Floats (`1e3`, `1.0`), out-of-range integers, and duplicate keys are all accepted or coerced by nlohmann but REJECTED by serde's derived Deserialize (`invalid type: floating point`, out-of-range, `duplicate field`), and process_action parses the body BEFORE it gates, so every such body 400s. Fail-closed.

4. SESSION-COUNTER DOUBLE-COUNT — DOES NOT OCCUR. The inner create_action receives TestRequest::default(), which has no X-Requesting-Domain, so dispatch_payment_with_amount takes its very first branch (`None => return GateOutcome::Proceed`) and returns before touching record_spending or increment_payment_rate_counter. Exactly one accounting event per /processAction call. The comment in process_action defending the synthetic inner request is correct as written.

5. X-USER-APPROVED DOUBLE REPLAY — CLOSED. consume_and_verify does `guard.remove(approval_id)` FIRST and only then checks expiry and body hash, so the entry is gone on every outcome including BodyMismatch and Expired — no probing oracle, no second use. (The missing endpoint binding is reported separately as finding 3.)

6. THE OTHER FOUR PRODUCTION TestRequest SITES — all four gate FIRST, with the caller's real &http_req and the caller's raw &body, before anything is built or spent. Verified individually: send_transaction (handlers.rs, dispatch_payment_with_amount "/transaction/send", and it correctly resolves the sendMax sweep amount from the balance so the sweep is priced rather than left at 0); peerpay_send ("/wallet/peerpay/send"); pay_402 ("/wallet/brc121/pay402"); paymail_send ("/wallet/paymail/send"). Each then calls create_action with TestRequest for the same stated reason — the inner body is re-serialised and is not the caller's, so forwarding http_req would make every X-User-Approved replay 403 on body_mismatch. That reasoning is sound and I could not break it.

7. PAGE-SUPPLIED TRUST HEADERS — sound on both transports. The IPC path (runIpcEngineCascade) constructs its header map from scratch and never merges page headers. The fetch path merges them but strips origin, x-requesting-domain, x-user-approved, x-browser-id, x-bsv-price-available, x-cert-approved-fields and the whole x-payment-* prefix first (kTrustHeaderExact). A page cannot inject its own price or its own approvalId.

8. ENDPOINT-STRING GAMES against IsPaymentEndpoint — fail-closed in the safe direction. A percent-encoded endpoint (`/%70rocessAction`) that actix still routes to process_action would miss C++'s substring match, so no X-Payment-* headers are stamped, PaymentCall::from_headers returns None, and dispatch_payment substitutes {0 sats, price_unavailable} and PROMPTS. There is no endpoint string that makes C++ price a call at 0-with-price-available while Rust routes it to a spender.

9. ONE FACTUAL ERROR, NOT A FINDING, but it should be corrected before it is trusted: the WARNING paragraph in handlers.rs :: send_transaction states "C++'s isPaymentEndpoint() does not list /transaction/send" and builds a fail-closed argument on that premise. PaymentCost.h :: IsPaymentEndpoint DOES list /transaction/send (and ExtractOutputSatoshis handles its {toAddress, amount, sendMax} shape) — the paragraph immediately below it says so. This is precisely the class of stale money-path comment this phase has already been burned by twice; it currently instructs a future reader that a live pricing path does not exist.

10. NOT INVESTIGATED, out of lens and flagged for whoever has it: whether a never-broadcast tx (`/processAction` with `broadcast:false`, or `/createAction` with `noSend:true`) leaves its inputs permanently reserved. The nosend branch of process_action returns without any rollback, while the broadcast-failure branch explicitly calls restore_spent_by_txid. If no reconcile task restores them, an approved dApp can lock UTXOs at 1 satoshi of priced cost per call. Pre-existing to /createAction, not introduced by today's fix, and it belongs to the WS1 reconcile workstream.

findings.mechanism: Answering my lens question literally: there IS a second dispatch path from a renderer to the wallet, and it is not IPC at all. `AddressHandler::Execute` constructs `WalletService walletService;` at function top and again inside the overlay branch, calling `walletService.generateAddress()` in-process; `IdentityHandler::Execute` does the same (`WalletService walletService;` then `isConnected()`/`isHealthy()`/`markWalletBackedUp()`). I could not construct a page that gets them. The defect is structural: the C2 gate is documented and reasoned about as THE renderer trust boundary for wallet reach, and it is not — any future widening of the injection predicate (or finding 1's framed internal document) silently escapes both gates with no log line and no audit record. lenses.ruledOut:
MY LENS'S HEADLINE ANSWER: the C2 gate IS in force on macOS, and V8 injection IS gated identically on both platforms. I found no `#ifdef _WIN32` around any gate. Specifics I verified myself rather than trusting comments:

1. NO PLATFORM GUARD ON THE GATE. `ResolveIpcOrigin`, `IpcMessageAllowedFromWebPage` and the default-deny check at the top of `SimpleHandler::OnProcessMessageReceived` contain zero preprocessor conditionals. `src/handlers/simple_handler.cpp` is in the unconditional `SOURCES` list in `cef-native/CMakeLists.txt`, not a WIN32 arm. `IsInternalOrigin` lives in `HttpRequestInterceptor.cpp`, which the APPLE branch explicitly appends. `PortConfig.h` (`OriginFromUrl`, `IsInternalFrontendUrl`, `IsLoopbackUrl`) has zero `_WIN32`/`__APPLE__` occurrences.

2. NO SECOND BROWSER-PROCESS DISPATCH PATH. `grep -rn "OnProcessMessageReceived"` across the whole tree yields exactly two implementations: `SimpleHandler` (browser side) and `SimpleRenderProcessHandler` (renderer side). `SimpleHandler` is the only `public CefClient` in the codebase. `simple_handler_mac.mm` contains only `PresentContextMenuMac` (NSMenu conversion) — no IPC. `my_overlay_render_handler.mm`/`.cpp` contain no `SendProcessMessage`, no `CefV8Handler`, no `OnContextCreated`. `process_helper_mac.mm` defines `HelperApp`, whose `GetRenderProcessHandler()` returns the SAME `SimpleRenderProcessHandler` the Windows `SimpleApp` uses. `cef_browser_shell_mac.mm` only *creates* messages (focus_address_bar, qr_screen_capture_result), never receives them. `TabManager_mac.mm :: CreateTab` and `TabManager.cpp :: CreateTab` both do `new SimpleHandler(role, window_id)` — same client, same gate, both platforms.

3. V8 INJECTION PARITY. `OnContextCreated` is one cross-platform function. The only `#ifdef`s inside it are (a) `hodosBrowser.platform` string, (b) the navigation object, (c) the address object — and (b)/(c) sit INSIDE the already-gated `isInternalPage || isOverlayBrowser` block. macOS is the wider arm on (c) (3 address functions vs Windows' 1), but still internal-only. `cefMessage`, `WALLET_CALL_BRIDGE_SCRIPT` and `CWI_SHIM_SCRIPT` are injected by identical, unconditional code on both platforms. macOS overlay URLs are all `http://127.0.0.1:5137/...` (17 sites in `cef_browser_shell_mac.mm`), so the internal-origin predicate resolves the same way there — no `file://` divergence.

4. THE INTERNAL RE-DISPATCH IS NOT A BYPASS. `simple_handler.cpp` calls its own `OnProcessMessageReceived(browser, browser->GetMainFrame(), PID_RENDERER, trigger)` once, in the `profiles_create` arm, to refresh the profile list. It re-enters the gate; `profiles_get_all` is not in the allowlist, so a web page cannot reach it either directly or via this re-entry.

5. TWO COMMENT CLAIMS I RE-GREPPED AND FOUND TRUE (given the project's history of false audit claims). (a) `PortConfig.h`'s assertion that nothing registers `hodos://` — `grep -rn "AddCustomScheme|OnRegisterCustomSchemes"` across `cef-native/` returns zero hits, so `IsInternalFrontendUrl`'s unconditional `hodos://` true-arm is unreachable by a committed frame URL, and `OriginFromUrl` returns empty for it anyway so `ResolveIpcOrigin` fails closed. (b) The allowlist's claim that its four names are the complete set emitted from injected page context — enumerating every `cefMessage.send('<name>')` literal in `cef-native/` yields exactly `cosmetic_class_id_query`, `find_result_js` (both `simple_handler.cpp`), `qr_found` (`QRScannerScript.h`) and `wallet_call`; the only `send_transaction` hit is inside the banner comment, not injected code.

6. FAIL-CLOSED PATHS I TRIED TO BREAK AND COULD NOT. `window.open('')` popup: main frame `about:blank`, `GetParent()` null, `GetMainFrame()` is itself, so `ResolveIpcOrigin` returns `opaque-origin.invalid` and the gate denies. `about:blank`/`data:`/`blob:` subframes of an external page: the ancestor cascade attributes them to the real parent. Userinfo (`http://127.0.0.1:5137@evil/`) and unanchored-scheme (`data:text/html,a://127.0.0.1:5137/`) both return empty from `OriginFromUrl` or the attacker host — the C1 fix holds.

DELIBERATELY NOT RE-REPORTED (already filed): `IsInternalOrigin` trusting any loopback port (panel #2 findings 10/15, port half deferred to Phase 5); `IsInternalOrigin("") == true` (owner decision, left as-is); the bare framability of `127.0.0.1:5137` (panel #1 §183, PHASE_CONTRACT.md:1218) — I report only the postMessage half that completes it into an exploit; the macOS `wallet_call` SSRF (relay E1); the ungated disclosure set.

lenses.lens: macOS close-prevention and the wallet overlay's trust posture — InstallClickOutsideMonitor, g_wallet_overlay_prevent_close, MainWindowDelegate::windowDidResignKey, NSWindow/NSEvent monitor pairs. Running on Windows: EVERY finding below is CODE_READING by construction. I could not execute the macOS tree; each finding names the exact Mac experiment that would settle it.

findings.title: macOS never sets g_wallet_overlay_prevent_close synchronously at creation and never clears it on destroy — the flag is 100% React-async-driven, the exact pattern CLAUDE.md forbids; four separate places assert the opposite
findings.mechanism: CLAUDE.md documents pattern #3 ("Wallet creation-time default — flag set in C++, cleared by React") because "a React-set flag cannot reliably guard" a focus-loss event. On Windows that default exists: `cef-native/src/handlers/simple_app.cpp :: CreateWalletOverlay` sets `g_wallet_overlay_prevent_close = true` right after the HWND is created, and `simple_app.cpp :: HideWalletOverlay` clears it — both inside the `#ifdef _WIN32` block that ends with `#endif // _WIN32` immediately after HideWalletOverlay, so neither compiles on macOS. On macOS the flag is DEFINED at `cef_browser_shell_mac.mm:287` (`bool g_wallet_overlay_prevent_close = false;`) and then never assigned anywhere in the macOS tree: a repo-wide grep for the symbol yields writes only in `simple_app.cpp` (Win-only) and `simple_handler.cpp` (the `wallet_prevent_close`/`wallet_allow_close` React IPC arms, plus the Windows-only `overlay_close` arm at ~4417). `cef_browser_shell_mac.mm :: CreateWalletOverlayWithSeparateProcess` creates the NSWindow, calls `makeKeyAndOrderFront:` and `InstallClickOutsideMonitor(g_wallet_overlay_window)` — all synchronous — while the flag is still whatever it was, i.e. false on the first open. Consequence (a): from window creation until `WalletPanelPage.tsx`'s `useEffect([preventClose])` first fires, any mouse-down outside the overlay reaches the local monitor at `OverlayHelpers_mac.mm :: InstallClickOutsideMonitor`, sees `!g_wallet_overlay_prevent_close`, and calls `CloseWalletOverlay()` — which `CloseBrowser(false)`s the wallet browser and closes the window. On Windows the same event only HIDES (keep-alive); on macOS it is a full destroy, so any in-flight setup state is unrecoverable. Consequence (b): the macOS `overlay_close` arm in `simple_handler.cpp` (the `#elif defined(__APPLE__)` block, role_=="wallet" → `CloseOverlayWindow(...)`, `g_wallet_overlay_window = nullptr`) and `cef_browser_shell_mac.mm :: HideWalletOverlay` both omit the `g_wallet_overlay_prevent_close = false` that their Windows twins perform — so a true flag survives overlay destruction and stays true until the next React mount happens to send `wallet_allow_close`. In that interval the flag is a stale global that gates finding #2's click swallow. Four artifacts assert the property the macOS code does not have: `frontend/src/pages/CLAUDE.md:182` ("The C++ side also sets `g_wallet_overlay_prevent_close = true` at overlay creation time (synchronous, no race)" — unqualified); `cef-native/src/handlers/CLAUDE.md:90` (overlay table row: "Keep-alive; prevent-close flag set on creation"); `cef-native/include/handlers/CLAUDE.md:89` (maps `CreateWalletOverlayWithSeparateProcess()` ↔ `CreateWalletOverlay()` as equivalents with no caveat); and the code comment at `WalletPanelPage.tsx:202-204` ("C++ sets g_wallet_overlay_prevent_close=true at overlay creation (synchronous). ... This avoids race conditions — C++ flag is always set before focus-loss events"). No test in `cef-native/tests/` touches the flag on either platform.

(2) Launch with `HODOS_DEV=1 ./mac_build_run.sh`, tail the log, click the wallet toolbar icon, and within the first ~300 ms (before `🔓 Wallet overlay close prevention DISABLED` appears) click on the page area. Expected observable if the finding holds: `OverlayHelpers: Click-outside detected (local) -- closing overlay` followed by `Closing wallet overlay (click-outside)` with NO preceding `🔒 Wallet overlay close prevention ENABLED`. NEGATIVE CONTROL: add `g_wallet_overlay_prevent_close = true;` immediately after `g_wallet_overlay_window = [[WalletOverlayWindow alloc] ...]` and re-run the same click — the close log must disappear. (3) For consequence (b): drive the panel to a PIN step (log shows `🔒 ... ENABLED`), press the panel's own X (`overlay_close`), then grep the log for `🔓 ... DISABLED` — its absence between the close and the next open confirms the stale-true window.

findings.title: macOS click-outside local monitor swallows EVERY outside mouse-down unconditionally, including while prevent-close blocks the close — so a PIN/mnemonic-state wallet panel eats the user's clicks on the payment approval prompt it also floats above
findings.mechanism: In `OverlayHelpers_mac.mm :: InstallClickOutsideMonitor`, the local `addLocalMonitorForEventsMatchingMask` handler returns the event only on the two early exits (`if (!overlay) return event;` and `if (clickedWindow == overlay) return event;`). Every other path falls through to a single terminal `return nil;  // Swallow the click event` that sits OUTSIDE the `dispatch_async` block. The prevent-close check lives inside that async block (`if (overlay == g_wallet_overlay_window) { if (!g_wallet_overlay_prevent_close) { CloseWalletOverlay(); } return; }`), so it can only suppress the CLOSE — it can never restore the click. Net effect: while the wallet overlay is open with `g_wallet_overlay_prevent_close == true` (which `WalletPanelPage.tsx` sets for `mnemonic !== null || (pinStep !== null && pendingAction !== null)` — i.e. recovery-phrase display and PIN-gated actions), every left/right/other mouse-down anywhere else in the application is discarded and the overlay also refuses to close. The app is click-wedged; only keyboard input still reaches anything. This collides with a load-bearing safeguard: the payment/permission approval prompt is the notification overlay, created at `NSNormalWindowLevel` (`cef_browser_shell_mac.mm`, `[g_notification_overlay_window setLevel:NSNormalWindowLevel]`), while the wallet overlay is created at `NSFloatingWindowLevel` (`[g_wallet_overlay_window setLevel:NSFloatingWindowLevel]`). So if a dApp-triggered approval prompt is raised while the user sits at a PIN step, the prompt is both potentially occluded by the higher-level wallet panel and unclickable — the user cannot press Block/Deny. It fails CLOSED (Approve is equally unclickable, and the request times out rather than auto-approving), which is why I rate this medium and not high: it degrades the user's ability to exercise the safeguard rather than bypassing it. Windows has no analogue — the `WH_MOUSE_LL` click-outside hook there is per-dropdown and the wallet's primary path is `WalletOverlayWndProc :: WM_ACTIVATE`, which returns 0 without consuming the user's click in another window.
findings.experiment: On a Mac: open the wallet panel and drive it into a prevent-close state (a PIN-gated action, so the log shows `🔒 Wallet overlay close prevention ENABLED`). Then click any toolbar button or page link. Then, from a dApp on an APPROVED domain, trigger an over-cap `createAction` so the notification overlay is raised while the PIN step is up; screenshot to record z-order versus the wallet panel, and attempt to click Block. NEGATIVE CONTROL: change the terminal `return nil;` to `return event;` when `overlay == g_wallet_overlay_window && g_wallet_overlay_prevent_close`, rebuild, repeat — the Block click must now register. Also confirm the un-clicked prompt resolves as DENY (not silent approve) by checking the Rust audit log.

findings.title: CloseOverlayWindow never removes the click-outside monitor, and CreateWalletOverlayWithSeparateProcess's destroy branch neither removes it nor CloseBrowser()s the old wallet browser — leaving a stale monitor over a closed NSWindow and an orphaned live wallet renderer
findings.mechanism: Two macOS teardown paths bypass `RemoveClickOutsideMonitor`. (1) `cef_browser_shell_mac.mm :: CloseOverlayWindow` does only `[parentWindow removeChildWindow:overlayWindow]` + `[overlayWindow close]`; it never touches `s_clickOutsideMonitors`. It is the function the `overlay_close` `__APPLE__` arm in `simple_handler.cpp` calls for role_=="wallet" (and every other role routed through that arm). (2) `cef_browser_shell_mac.mm :: CreateWalletOverlayWithSeparateProcess`'s keep-alive-less destroy branch does `[g_wallet_overlay_window close]; g_wallet_overlay_window = nullptr;` with no `RemoveClickOutsideMonitor` and — unlike `CloseWalletOverlay` — no `wallet_browser->GetHost()->CloseBrowser(false)` and no `removeChildWindow`. Consequences: the monitor pair stays registered against a dangling `NSWindow* __unsafe_unretained unsafeOverlay` (the window is `setReleasedWhenClosed:NO` and nothing releases it, so the pointer stays allocated rather than crashing). On the next mouse-down anywhere, the stale handler runs: `clickedWindow != overlay`, the async block finds `overlay != g_wallet_overlay_window` (now nullptr or a new window) and finds the key STILL in `GetMonitorDict()` — so it does not take the stale-callback early return, and instead calls `RemoveClickOutsideMonitor(overlay); [overlay close];` on an already-closed window — while the handler has already returned `nil`, eating that click. It self-heals after one click, so this is a one-click-per-cycle UX defect, not a wedge. The second half is worse than the first: the orphaned wallet CefBrowser from path (2) is never closed, so a renderer holding wallet-panel state (and, if the destroy happened during setup, the rendered recovery phrase in its DOM) keeps running headless for the rest of the process lifetime with no window and no way for the user to see or dismiss it. Windows has no equivalent: `CreateWalletOverlay` takes the keep-alive early return instead of destroying, and the Windows `overlay_close` arm explicitly clears the HWND, the mouse hook (for settings) and the prevent-close flag.
findings.experiment: On a Mac, run with the Logger at DEBUG. (a) Open the wallet panel, close it with the panel's own X button (`overlay_close`), then click once on the page. Expected if the finding holds: `OverlayHelpers: Click-outside detected (local) -- closing overlay` fires for a window that is already gone, `OverlayHelpers: Removed click-outside monitors` follows, and the click does not reach the page. Absence of `OverlayHelpers: Removed click-outside monitors` between the X press and that click confirms CloseOverlayWindow skipped it. NEGATIVE CONTROL: add `RemoveClickOutsideMonitor(overlayWindow);` at the top of `CloseOverlayWindow`, rebuild — the stray detection log and the eaten click must both disappear. (b) For the orphaned browser: with the wallet panel HIDDEN-but-alive (trigger the QR screen-capture path, which calls HideWalletOverlay), send `toggle_wallet_panel` from the BRC-100 auth overlay button (`BRC100AuthOverlayRoot.tsx:1079`) so the destroy branch runs; then count wallet-role renderer processes with `ps aux | grep -c 'Helper (Renderer)'` before and after, and confirm no `Closing wallet overlay (click-outside)` / CloseBrowser log accompanied the destroy.

findings.title: On macOS nothing dismisses the wallet panel when the application is deactivated — no delegate on the wallet NSWindow and an explicit exemption in the app-focus-loss handler — where Windows hides it; the comment claiming parity with WM_ACTIVATEAPP is false
findings.mechanism: Windows has two focus-driven dismissals for the wallet overlay: `cef_browser_shell.cpp :: WalletOverlayWndProc` `WM_ACTIVATE(WA_INACTIVE)` (the documented PRIMARY path) and the main WndProc's `WM_ACTIVATEAPP`, which calls `HideWalletOverlay()` unless `g_wallet_overlay_prevent_close || g_file_dialog_active`. macOS has neither. `[g_main_window setDelegate:[[MainWindowDelegate alloc] init]]` is the only `setDelegate` call in `cef_browser_shell_mac.mm` — `CreateWalletOverlayWithSeparateProcess` sets no delegate on `g_wallet_overlay_window`, so there is no `windowDidResignKey` for the wallet window at all; and `MainWindowDelegate::windowDidResignKey` only logs the first responder. The app-level handler, `OverlayHelpers_mac.mm :: InstallAppFocusLossHandler` (NSApplicationDidResignActiveNotification), closes settings-menu, three-dot menu, bookmarks, site-info and tab-list overlays and then explicitly skips the wallet with the comment "Wallet overlay is NOT closed here. It has the prevent-close exemption ... This matches the Windows WM_ACTIVATEAPP behavior where wallet is guarded by g_wallet_overlay_prevent_close." That comment asserts a property the code does not have: Windows CLOSES the wallet on WM_ACTIVATEAPP and merely SKIPS the close when the flag is set; macOS never closes it, flag or no flag, and does not read the flag on this path. So the only macOS dismissal is a mouse-down (the global NSEvent monitor) — Cmd+Tab, Spotlight, Mission Control and Exposé leave the panel up. Combined with `setLevel:NSFloatingWindowLevel` and no `hidesOnDeactivate` anywhere in the file (grep returns zero hits; the AppKit default for NSWindow, unlike NSPanel, is NO), the panel plausibly renders ABOVE the newly-focused application. What is exposed in the ordinary (non-prevent-close) case is the wallet panel's balance, receive addresses, activity list and transaction form — a privacy leak into screen shares and screen recordings that Windows does not have. I deliberately do NOT claim a mnemonic divergence here: during recovery-phrase display `preventClose` is true, and Windows also keeps the overlay up in that state, so the two platforms agree on the mnemonic case by design. I also do not assert the final z-order — `addChildWindow:ordered:NSWindowAbove` runs after `setLevel:` and AppKit's child-window level semantics are the open question.
findings.experiment: On a Mac: open the wallet panel showing a non-zero balance and a receive address (prevent-close NOT engaged — confirm `🔓 Wallet overlay close prevention DISABLED` in the log). Press Cmd+Tab to Safari WITHOUT clicking. Then run `screencapture -x /tmp/z.png` and inspect: if the wallet panel's balance and address are legible over Safari, both halves of the finding hold (not dismissed AND rendering above the foreground app). If the panel is behind Safari but still on screen in Mission Control, only the first half holds. NEGATIVE CONTROL for the parity claim: run the identical sequence on Windows with Alt+Tab — the log must show `Hiding wallet overlay due to app focus loss` and the panel must vanish, proving the platforms differ. Second control: add `[g_wallet_overlay_window setHidesOnDeactivate:YES]` in CreateWalletOverlayWithSeparateProcess, rebuild, repeat the Cmd+Tab — the panel must disappear from the screenshot.

lenses.ruledOut:
Things I checked in this lens and found SOUND (all code reading; I am on Windows and could not execute the macOS tree):

1. **`wallet_allow_close` / `wallet_prevent_close` are NOT web-reachable.** I re-grepped the C2 gate rather than trusting the phase notes. `simple_handler.cpp :: IpcMessageAllowedFromWebPage` allows exactly four names — `wallet_call`, `cosmetic_class_id_query`, `find_result_js`, `qr_found` — and the default-deny check `if (!IsInternalOrigin(ipcOrigin) && !IpcMessageAllowedFromWebPage(message_name)) return true;` sits at the very top of `OnProcessMessageReceived`, before every arm. So a hostile page cannot clear the prevent-close flag out from under a recovery-phrase screen, and cannot drive `toggle_wallet_panel` / `overlay_show_wallet` / `overlay_close` to destroy an overlay. `ResolveIpcOrigin` maps an unresolvable frame to `opaque-origin.invalid` rather than the empty string, so the old `IsInternalOrigin("")==true` hazard does not reach this gate. The prevent-close subsystem is reachable only from internal overlay origins.

2. **`MainWindowDelegate::windowDidResignKey` is inert, and that is not itself a defect** — it only logs the first responder. It is the *absence* of a wallet-window delegate that matters, which I report as finding #4 rather than double-counting here.

3. **The mnemonic-exposure case is at parity, not a macOS regression.** I expected to find that macOS leaves a recovery phrase on screen where Windows hides it. It does not: during mnemonic display `WalletPanelPage.tsx`'s `preventClose` is true, and the Windows `WM_ACTIVATEAPP` arm explicitly *keeps* the overlay open when the flag is set. Both platforms deliberately keep the phrase visible across app switches so the user can transcribe it. I dropped that claim.

4. **The backup overlay is also at parity.** `BackupOverlayRoot.tsx` renders `wallet.mnemonic`, and on macOS `g_backup_overlay_window` is `NSNormalWindowLevel` and absent from `InstallAppFocusLossHandler`'s close list — but the Windows `WM_ACTIVATEAPP` arm does not touch the backup overlay either. No divergence.

5. **The header wallet icon cannot be used to destroy a prevent-close overlay.** I chased this as a potential mnemonic-loss path: macOS `toggle_wallet_panel` routes to `CreateWalletOverlayWithSeparateProcess`, whose destroy branch fires unconditionally without consulting `g_wallet_overlay_prevent_close` (where Windows hides keep-alive). But the click that would reach the header is swallowed first by the wallet's own local monitor, so the IPC never fires from a mouse. I could not construct a keyboard route to it. Reported only as a contributing mechanism inside finding #3, not as a standalone mnemonic-loss claim.

6. **The QR screen-capture path restores the monitor correctly.** `FinishQRScreenCaptureMacOS` calls `ShowWalletOverlay()` on all four exits (cancelled, too-small, null image, normal), and `ShowWalletOverlay` re-runs `InstallClickOutsideMonitor`, which begins with `RemoveClickOutsideMonitor`. No monitor leak on that path.

7. **`InstallClickOutsideMonitor` is idempotent** — the leading `RemoveClickOutsideMonitor(overlayWindow)` prevents double-install, so repeated Show calls do not stack monitor pairs.

8. **No test in `cef-native/tests/` covers overlay close prevention on either platform**, so there is no harness here that would pass with the feature removed — there is no harness at all. That is a coverage gap rather than a false-green, and I note it rather than count it as a finding.

lenses.lens: Break TODAY's PaymentCost.h change — the substring `IsPaymentEndpoint` list, and the `ExtractOutputSatoshis` / `IsSendMaxAnywhere` body-shape rule — against the invariant "no fund-mover may ever be priced at 0 cents with priceAvailable=true". findings.title: /wallet/pay402 is absent from IsPaymentEndpoint, and pay_402's gate is conditional on exactly the headers that absence guarantees are missing → unmetered, unprompted, gold-pill-free spend from any connected dApp
findings.mechanism:
THE INVERSION. Every other gated endpoint fails CLOSED when the X-Payment-* headers are absent: `PaymentCall::from_headers` returns None and `dispatch_payment` substitutes `bsv_price_available=false`, which matrix_c.rs turns into a PriceUnavailable prompt. `pay_402` is the one handler that does not do that — it wraps the whole `dispatch_payment` call in `let brc121_engine_headers_present = http_req.headers().contains_key("X-Payment-Satoshis") || http_req.headers().contains_key("X-User-Approved"); if brc121_engine_headers_present { ... }`. A request that carries neither header does not get a fail-closed prompt; it gets NO GATE AT ALL.

What guarantees the headers are absent is PaymentCost.h. `runIpcEngineCascade` stamps X-Browser-Id / X-Payment-Satoshis / X-Payment-Cents / X-Bsv-Price-Available `if (isPaymentKind)` only, and `isPaymentKind = hodos::IsPaymentEndpoint(endpoint)`. `/wallet/pay402` matches none of the seven substrings in that list. So a page-initiated call arrives header-free by construction, and the gate self-disables. (The legitimate BRC-121 chain stamps the headers itself in HttpRequestInterceptor.cpp, `payHeaders["X-Payment-Satoshis"]` — which is why the real flow has always looked gated. The "rollout gate: engage ONLY when the CEF interceptor sends the engine headers" comment describes a dormancy switch that was never removed after the paired C++ flip landed.)

findings.title: Two in-code WARNINGs on the money path now assert the opposite of what PaymentCost.h does — 'isPaymentEndpoint() does not list this route, so an external send always prompts'
findings.mechanism:
`send_transaction` carries a block-comment WARNING addressed to future maintainers: "external callers reach dispatch_payment WITHOUT X-Payment-* headers, because C++'s isPaymentEndpoint() does not list /transaction/send. That path is fail-closed by design … So an external send always prompts and can never silently exceed a cap." `peerpay_send` carries the mirror claim: "C++'s isPaymentEndpoint() does not list this route, so external callers arrive with no X-Payment-* headers and are fail-closed into a price_unavailable prompt."

Both statements are false as of the current tree. `hodos::IsPaymentEndpoint` lists `/transaction/send`, `/wallet/peerpay/send` and `/wallet/paymail/send`, and `ExtractOutputSatoshis` has arms for both `{toAddress, amount}` and `{amount_satoshis}`. The paired change was done correctly — but the comments were not updated, so both routes are now silent-eligible under the cap while the code next to them still says they can never be.

The harm is not to today's behaviour, it is to the next reviewer. This exact position in the tree has already produced two commit messages asserting audits that were demonstrably false and one banner comment claiming a property the code did not have; a reviewer who trusts either of these WARNINGs will conclude a route is fail-closed when it is silent-eligible, and will not re-derive it. It is also the precise class of statement that PaymentCost.h's own header banner exists to make testable.

findings.title: An internal-frontend document embedded as a SUBFRAME of a hostile page gets full wallet-internal trust: no frame-ancestors, and ResolveIpcOrigin never looks at the top-level document
findings.mechanism: ResolveIpcOrigin sets `origin = hodos::OriginFromUrl(frame->GetURL())` and, when that is non-empty, RETURNS IT — the ancestor loop (`for f = frame->GetParent(); f && origin.empty()`) and the `browser->GetMainFrame()` fallback are both guarded on `origin.empty()`, so they never run for a frame that has its own real origin. A subframe committed at http://127.0.0.1:5137/... therefore resolves to "127.0.0.1:5137" regardless of what the top-level document is. That value passes IsInternalOrigin, so the C2 default-deny gate at the top of OnProcessMessageReceived admits EVERY message name (send_transaction, add_domain_permission, add_domain_permission_advanced, grant_scoped_permission, permission_response, wallet_call, …), and wallet_call routes through HandleIpcWalletCall -> runIpcCallDirect, which deliberately omits X-Requesting-Domain; Rust's domain_trust_mw then takes its `None => return Ok(next.call(req).await?)` branch, i.e. NO gate runs at all — no domain approval, no per-tx/per-session cap, no gold pill. Nothing stops the framing: I grepped all of cef-native for Content-Security-Policy / X-Frame-Options / frame-ancestors and there are ZERO matches; LocalFileResourceRequestHandler::GetResourceHandler returns `new CefStreamResourceHandler(mime, stream)` with only a MIME type, and frontend/index.html carries no CSP meta. In a RELEASE build nothing needs to be listening on 5137 — today's G1 arm in GetResourceRequestHandler serves {app}\frontend from disk for any URL where hodos::IsInternalFrontendUrl is true, and that arm is not gated on role_ or frame->IsMain(), so it fires for subframe requests inside an ordinary tab. There is no OnBeforeSubframeNavigation implementation anywhere in cef-native (grepped: no matches) and OnBeforeBrowse never blocks a navigation. In the renderer, SimpleRenderProcessHandler::OnContextCreated computes isInternalPage/isOverlayBrowser from `frame->GetURL()` alone, so the framed document also receives hodosBrowser.identity/.navigation/.history. attacker input -> `<iframe src="http://127.0.0.1:5137/brc100-auth?type=payment&domain=…&requestId=…">` (BRC100AuthOverlayRoot::applyParams builds the ENTIRE prompt, including the requestId that keys the C++ callback, from URL params) rendered at opacity 0 over a decoy button -> one user click inside the attacker's page runs a fully-trusted, completely ungated wallet action. Cross-origin script access is NOT available to the attacker, so the money-moving step needs that one click (UI redress) — I am not claiming a zero-click break.

findings.title: IsInternalOrigin trusts ANY loopback port, so any local HTTP server the user visits in Hodos gets a header-free, completely ungated wallet — while IsInternalFrontendUrl requires :5137. The money path uses the looser predicate.
findings.mechanism: I compiled the real cef-native/include/core/PortConfig.h plus a verbatim copy of HttpRequestInterceptor.cpp::IsInternalOrigin with MSVC 14.44 and ran it. MEASURED: `http://localhost:3000/` -> origin `localhost:3000`, IsInternalFrontendUrl=0, IsInternalOrigin=1. `http://127.0.0.1:31302/x` -> origin `127.0.0.1:31302`, IsInternalFrontendUrl=0, IsInternalOrigin=1. So the two predicates DISAGREE, and the money path consults the looser one: HandleIpcWalletCall's first branch is `if (IsInternalOrigin(origin)) { runIpcCallDirect(...); return; }`, and runIpcCallDirect's own comment states the intent plainly — "Internal == wallet-internal (the first-party UI served from 127.0.0.1:5137, or any loopback caller), and it MUST reach Rust header-free". Its header map is `{Content-Type: application/json}` and X-Requesting-Domain is stamped only `if (!origin.empty() && !IsInternalOrigin(origin))` — never on this path. Rust's domain_trust_mw reads X-Requesting-Domain and, absent, returns `next.call(req)` immediately, so NOTHING runs: not the §4k permission-surface refusal, not the reveal-mnemonic/wallet-settings first-party arms landed in c8558dc, not dispatch_payment. AsyncWalletResourceHandler::Open has the same branch ("🔒 Internal origin … — bypassing domain check"). CODE_READING for reachability: a remote page cannot mint a loopback origin, but any locally-installed web UI (dev server, Jupyter/Grafana-class app, game/vendor launcher, Electron helper) the user opens in Hodos is, by this predicate, indistinguishable from the wallet UI itself — one XSS or one attacker-controlled HTML response on any such port yields POST /wallet/reveal-mnemonic and unprompted createAction with no modal and no gold pill.

Escalate to `/wallet/reveal-mnemonic` and discriminate by status code alone (403 = gate ran, 401/200 = handler ran). findings.title: hodos::IsWalletHostPort is still an UNANCHORED substring search, so any page can force an arbitrary https request to be downgraded to plaintext http and/or re-routed into the wallet by putting "127.0.0.1:31301" in its own query string
findings.mechanism: MEASURED with the compiled header: `hodos::IsWalletHostPort("https://evil.com/?q=127.0.0.1:31301")` == 1 and `IsWalletHostPort("https://evil.com/?q=localhost:31301")` == 1 — it is `url.find(...) != npos` on the whole URL, the exact pattern PortConfig.h's own trust-boundary banner forbids for the 5137 gate but never applied to these two helpers. CODE_READING for the chain: SimpleHandler::GetResourceRequestHandler dispatches on `hodos::IsWalletHostPort(url) || hodos::IsLoopbackHostPort(url,"3321"|"2121"|"8080")` — all four unanchored — so `https://victim.example/api/decrypt?q=127.0.0.1:31301` is handed to HttpRequestInterceptor. Inside HttpRequestInterceptor::GetResourceHandler, `redirectPort` no-ops (the target port string is already present), then the scheme-downgrade arm fires: `if (url.rfind("https://",0)==0 && hodos::IsWalletHostPort(url)) { url = "http://" + url.substr(8); request->SetURL(url); }` — mutating an https request to a THIRD-PARTY host into cleartext, which is precisely what the comment two lines above says must never happen ("Downgrade ONLY once the URL is already OUR wallet host:port… this must not become a general https->http rewrite"). Then isWalletEndpoint matches on bare path substrings including `/wallet/`, `/encrypt`, `/decrypt`, `/getVersion`, so the request is not sent to victim.example at all: endpoint is taken as the path and AsyncWalletResourceHandler serves it from OUR wallet, delivering the wallet's bytes as a SAME-ORIGIN response to the requesting page — browser CORS never applies. Rust still sees the correct X-Requesting-Domain (extractDomain reads the main frame, unaffected), so the Rust gates survive; the new capabilities are (a) TLS strip on attacker-chosen third-party URLs, cookies attached, and (b) a CORS-free read channel to whatever the Rust gate does allow.
findings.experiment: From a page on a public https origin, issue `fetch('https://<a-host-you-control-with-plaintext-logging>/x?q=127.0.0.1:31301',{mode:'no-cors'})` and watch the wire (Wireshark or a plaintext listener on :80). This settles the one thing I could NOT determine from source — whether CEF honours `CefRequest::SetURL` inside GetResourceHandler (docs steer mutation to OnBeforeResourceLoad); if it does not, the downgrade half is refuted and only the re-route half stands. Separately: `fetch('https://<your-host>/api/decrypt?q=127.0.0.1:31301')` and check whether the response body is the wallet's (or a wallet error envelope) rather than your server's — your server's access log staying empty is the tell. NEGATIVE CONTROL: drop the `?q=` and confirm both requests behave normally over TLS to your host.

findings.title: OriginFromUrl's authority scan stops only at '/', '?', '#' — a backslash, TAB, LF or SPACE before the last '@' turns a hostile URL into an internal one (latent; every caller today passes a Chromium-canonicalized spec)
findings.mechanism: MEASURED with the compiled header: OriginFromUrl("http://evil.com\\@127.0.0.1:5137/") == "127.0.0.1:5137", and identically for a TAB, an LF and a SPACE in place of the backslash — IsInternalFrontendUrl returns 1 and IsInternalOrigin returns 1 for all four. The cause is that the authority terminator set is only {'/','?','#'} while the userinfo rule discards everything through the LAST '@', so any character that a real URL parser treats as an authority terminator but this one does not lets an attacker append a fake authority. CODE_READING for reachability: every live caller I traced passes a Chromium-canonicalized spec — ResolveIpcOrigin and extractDomain use CefFrame::GetURL()/CefRequest::GetReferrerURL(), GetResourceRequestHandler uses CefRequest::GetURL(), OnContextCreated uses frame->GetURL() — and WHATWG canonicalization converts '\\' to '/', strips TAB/CR/LF and percent-encodes SPACE, so I found NO path that reaches OriginFromUrl with a non-canonical string. This is a latent hardening gap, not a live exploit, and I am explicitly not claiming otherwise. Same family, also MEASURED: IsInternalFrontendUrl("hodos://evil.com/") == 1 (the historical prefix arm returns true before OriginFromUrl is consulted, and cef-native/tests/port_config_origin_test.cpp asserts that behaviour as correct) — unreachable today because I grepped all of cef-native and there is no AddCustomScheme / OnRegisterCustomSchemes anywhere, confirming PortConfig.h's claim; NavigationHandler.cpp rewrites hodos:// to http://127.0.0.1:5137/ before navigation. Also note the port_config_origin_test.cpp suite contains no backslash, whitespace or 'hodos://evil.com' case, so it would pass unchanged with this gap present.

For reachability, instrument ResolveIpcOrigin to log its raw input and browse a corpus of adversarial URLs — if no non-canonical spec is ever observed, the finding stays latent, which is the expected outcome.

lenses.ruledOut:
Checked and found SOUND (all MEASURED against the compiled real header unless noted):

1. IsInternalOrigin("") still returns true — CONFIRMED MEASURED — but I could not find anyone who can still reach it with an empty string. Both live derivations now fail closed to the RFC-2606 sentinel before the call: ResolveIpcOrigin ends `if (origin.empty()) origin = "opaque-origin.invalid"`, and HttpRequestInterceptor::extractDomain does the same. The wallet_call arm binds `const std::string& origin = ipcOrigin` and does not re-derive. requestDomain_ has exactly one source — both `new AsyncWalletResourceHandler(...)` sites in GetResourceHandler pass extractDomain's result. runIpcCallDirect's `if (!origin.empty() && !IsInternalOrigin(origin))` is dead-guarded for the same reason. MEASURED: IsInternalOrigin("opaque-origin.invalid") == 0. The empty-string arm is now latent only; I'd still delete it, but it is not a finding.

2. Uppercase/mixed scheme fails CLOSED, not open: OriginFromUrl("HTTP://127.0.0.1:5137/") and ("Http://…") both return "" (rfind is case-sensitive) -> IsInternalFrontendUrl 0, IsLoopbackUrl 0 -> sentinel -> external. Same for "HODOS://evil.com/" (0, vs 1 for lowercase). Unreachable anyway since Chromium lowercases the scheme.

3. Uppercase host: "http://LOCALHOST:5137/" -> origin "LOCALHOST:5137", internal 0. Fails closed.

4. Trailing dots: "http://localhost.:5137/" and "http://127.0.0.1.:5137/" -> internal 0, loopback 0 (AuthorityHasHost requires the next char be ':' or end). Fails closed.

5. IPv6: "http://[::1]:5137/" -> internal 0, loopback 1 (correct — [::1] is in IsLoopbackUrl but deliberately not in IsInternalFrontendUrl); "http://[::ffff:127.0.0.1]:5137/" -> both 0. No bracket/colon confusion turns hostile into internal.

6. Alternate IPv4 spellings: "http://127.1:5137/" and "http://2130706433:5137/" -> internal 0, loopback 0. Fails closed here, and Chromium canonicalizes them to dotted-quad upstream so the legitimate case still works.

7. Multi-'@' userinfo behaves correctly: "http://user@evil.com@127.0.0.1:5137/" -> "127.0.0.1:5137" (rfind('@') — correct per RFC 3986, the LAST '@' really does end userinfo; Chromium agrees). "http://127.0.0.1:5137%2f@evil.com/" -> "evil.com". "http://:@127.0.0.1:5137/" -> "127.0.0.1:5137". The panel-#2 fix holds.

8. Query/fragment poisoning is closed in the direction that matters: "https://evil.com/?q=127.0.0.1:31301" and "…#…" -> origin "evil.com", internal 0, loopback 0. (It is NOT closed for IsWalletHostPort — that is finding 3.)

9. Today's G1 arm itself: `hodos::IsInternalFrontendUrl(url) && IsFrontendAvailable(frontend_dir)` in GetResourceRequestHandler is a genuine prefix/authority match; "https://example.com/?x=127.0.0.1:5137" no longer reaches LocalFileResourceRequestHandler. LocalFileResourceRequestHandler::ExtractPath additionally rejects "..", drive-letter and rooted paths, so I found no traversal out of {app}\frontend.

11. Not reported (too weak to rank): OnLoadingStateChange's history-exclusion test `url.find("http://127.0.0.1:5137") != 0` is a bare prefix, so a userinfo URL is wrongly EXCLUDED from history (privacy-negative but not money), and it omits the localhost:5137 spelling. The farbling per-site lookup in OnBeforeBrowse and the adblock per-site lookup in GetResourceRequestHandler both still hand-roll `find("://")` with no scheme anchor and no userinfo strip — neither is on the money path, but they are the two remaining un-migrated copies of the derivation.

findings.title: createAction options.sendWith broadcasts arbitrary local txids, and the payment gate prices it at zero
findings.mechanism: An approved dApp calls window.CWI.createAction({outputs:[{satoshis:1,...}], options:{sendWith:["<any txid>"]}}). C++ computePaymentCost -> ExtractOutputSatoshis(body) only sums outputs[].satoshis, so X-Payment-* is stamped as 1 sat / ~0 cents; dispatch_payment sees a value far under per_tx_limit_cents (default 100) and auto-approves SILENTLY. handlers.rs :: create_action_internal then enters `if is_send_with` and, for every txid in the array, looks it up in parent_transactions (NO status filter at all) or falls back to TransactionRepository::get_local_parent_tx, whose only filter is `status != 'completed'`, and calls broadcast_transaction on the raw hex. Nothing checks that the tx is nosend, that it belongs to this dApp, that it was not aborted, or that it was not already marked failed. Note this is strictly weaker than the sibling handler: broadcast_nosend DOES enforce `status == 'nosend'`; sendWith enforces nothing. findings.mechanism: abort_action's only guard is `ActionStatus::Confirmed` (and an early return for already-Aborted). A transaction in DB status 'sending' or 'unproven' maps through TransactionStatus::to_action_status to Signed/Unconfirmed, so the guard does not fire, and abort_action calls update_status(txid, ActionStatus::Aborted). TransactionStatus::from_legacy maps `(ActionStatus::Aborted, _) => TransactionStatus::Nosend`, so the DB row for a transaction that is already in the mempool becomes status='nosend'. TaskCheckForProofs selects status IN ('sending','unproven','nosend') and applies NOSEND_TIMEOUT_SECS = 600 to nosend rows instead of UNPROVEN_TIMEOUT_SECS = 6h. age_secs is measured from created_at, so any tx broadcast more than 10 minutes ago is instantly `is_timed_out`; the oracle sees it in the mempool but unconfirmed (`Present { any_confirmed: false }`) and takes the explicit "in mempool but past timeout — marking failed" branch. mark_failed then disables the change outputs (balance drops by the change amount) and calls restore_spent_by_txid, marking the inputs of a transaction that is on its way into a block spendable again. lenses.ruledOut:
All five findings are CODE_READING. I am on Windows, this was a read-only investigation, and I executed nothing — no wallet was run, no request was issued, no test was compiled. Every citation was re-grepped in this session rather than taken from a comment or a prior claim; where a comment and the code disagreed (debug_broadcast_nosend) I report the code.

Checked and found SOUND — these are real defenses, not gaps:
- `spends` cannot hijack a wallet input. sign_action bounds-checks `idx < tx.inputs.len()`, and the wallet-signing loop writes index `num_user_inputs + wallet_idx` unconditionally after the spends pass, overwriting anything the caller put there. `spends_applied` is consulted only inside the user-input loop, whose indices are 0..num_user_inputs. No path lets caller-supplied script bytes survive on a wallet input.
- Basket-insertion rows cannot poison coin selection. `get_spendable_by_user` requires `derivation_prefix IS NOT NULL` and basket name 'default'/NULL; insertion passes None/None. So the "feed the signer an unspendable UTXO and brick every future spend" attack does NOT work. (The balance query is the one that lacks the filter — finding 5.)
- The production `broadcast_nosend` guard is real: `Ok((Some(rt), status)) if status == "nosend"`, with an explicit skipped-response arm for every other status. Only the /wallet/debug/ twin dropped it.
- internalize_action does verify the transaction on-chain (`check_tx_exists_on_chain`) before storing, so wholly fabricated txids/outputs are rejected — the attacker must supply a genuine on-chain transaction.
- PENDING_TRANSACTIONS is cleaned up when `unsigned_inputs.is_empty()`, so signAction against a completed reference 404s. The exposure is confined to created-but-unsigned and phase-1-parked actions.
- /listActions does NOT leak the signed raw transaction. I chased the "reconstruct the raw tx from inputs/outputs/version/lockTime and replay it through internalizeAction" idea and it fails: `update_txid` re-inserts the OLD StoredAction's inputs, so `transaction_inputs.script` keeps the pre-signing EMPTY scriptSigs, and `list_actions` never emits raw_tx. Dropped.
- abort_action correctly refuses a 'completed'/Confirmed transaction, so the finding-2 window closes once a block confirms.
- `domain_trust_mw`'s §4k subtree gate is correct as written for what it covers: it decodes the path with the same decoder actix routes on, matches `/domain/` and `/wallet/session` as PREFIXES, and the self-revoke carve-out is properly narrowed (DELETE only, exact path, target domain must equal requesting domain). I tried to find an encoding or method that slips past it and did not.
- I did not re-report the known-open base facts (73 ungated routes, the disclosure set, is_permission_surface being a string list, macOS SSRF). Findings 1-5 are specific money-moving or state-corrupting consequences, each with its own handler and its own fix.

A web page sends cefMessage.send('wallet_call',[reqId,name,'/createAction','{}', METHOD]) where METHOD = "GET /wallet/export HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:31301

X". The C2 default-deny gate passes it ('wallet_call' is allowlisted). simple_handler.cpp reads args->GetString(4) into httpMethod with NO validation and forwards to HandleIpcWalletCall → runIpcEngineCascade (external origin) → dispatchWalletHttpByMethod: METHOD is neither exactly "GET" nor "POST", so it takes the else branch → SyncHttpClient::Request → `curl_easy_setopt(curl, CURLOPT_CUSTOMREQUEST, method.c_str())` (SyncHttpClient.cpp:537, __APPLE__ arm). libcurl does NOT sanitize CRLF in CUSTOMREQUEST. MEASURED against this box's libcurl 8.2.1: the bytes on the wire become a COMPLETE first request `GET /wallet/export HTTP/1.1
Host:...

` carrying NO X-Requesting-Domain, with the real curl-built request (bearing X-Requesting-Domain: evil.com) demoted to a second, garbled request. Rust's domain_trust middleware treats a request with no X-Requesting-Domain as wallet-internal/trusted, so /wallet/export returns the BIP39 recovery phrase; libcurl reads that first response into response.body, which is delivered back to the page via wallet_response IPC.
